chunks.title: Visual acuity: Snellen basics
chunks.tldr: Visual acuity = the smallest letter you can read. Normal is 6/6 (same as 20/20).
points: Snellen chart = black letters on white, read from a set distance (6 m).
Test the worse eye first, cover the other eye, and push the patient to read every letter they can.
BCVA (best-corrected VA) = best they can see with the right glasses.
Pinhole (~1 mm hole) cancels out refractive error. If VA gets better with pinhole → it's a glasses problem.
Pinhole can make vision worse in macular disease or posterior lens opacity.
Using both eyes together usually beats the better eye alone.
chunks.hook: Pinhole helps = 'just needs glasses'. Pinhole doesn't help = look for disease.
pearls: If VA is worse than 6/6, always repeat with a pinhole.

cards.q: VA 6/18 improves to 6/6 with pinhole. What's the likely cause?
Which eye do you test first?
cards.a: The eye the patient says is worse.

chunks.title: Very poor vision: CF, HM, PL
chunks.tldr: If they can't read the top letter, step down: CF → HM → PL → NPL.
points: CF (counts fingers): can count your fingers, usually at 1 metre. Write down the distance.
HM (hand movements): can tell your hand is moving just in front of them.
PL (perception of light): sees light only, no shapes. Cover the other eye really well.
Light projection: can they tell which direction the light comes from? With just a dense cataract they should get it right. If they get directions wrong → think retina or optic nerve problem.
chunks.hook: Going down the ladder: Fingers → Hand → Light. Each step needs less vision.

cards.q: Dense cataract, PL vision. Should light projection be accurate?
cards.a: Yes. Wrong projection suggests retinal or optic nerve disease behind the cataract.

cards.q: Order the poor-vision levels from best to worst.

chunks.title: LogMAR charts (the research chart)
chunks.tldr: LogMAR is a fairer, more accurate chart. 6/6 = 0.00, 6/60 = 1.00. Lower score = better vision.
points: LogMAR = log of the Minimum Angle of Resolution. 6/6 → MAR 1 → log = 0.
6/12 → MAR 2 → 0.30. 6/60 → MAR 10 → 1.00. Better than 6/6 gives a negative number.
Each row has 5 letters. Each row = 0.1, so each letter = 0.02. Every letter counts.
Keep going until they get half a line wrong.
Bailey–Lovie chart: 6 m. ETDRS chart: 4 m, square Sloan letters.
Better than Snellen: same number of letters on every row (equal 'crowding'), evenly spaced. Downside: takes longer.
chunks.hook: LogMAR is like golf: lower score wins.
pearls: Clinical trials use logMAR because it's the most accurate VA test.

cards.q: What is 6/60 in logMAR?
How much is one letter worth on a logMAR chart?

chunks.title: Near vision & contrast sensitivity
chunks.tldr: Near vision is a sensitive test for macular disease. Contrast sensitivity picks up problems even when VA is still normal.
points: Near VA: wear reading glasses, measure the reading distance, record smallest print for each eye, then both eyes.
Contrast sensitivity = seeing grey on grey, not just black on white.
Contrast can drop while VA stays normal in: amblyopia, optic neuropathy, some cataracts, higher-order aberrations.
Use it when the patient says 'I see badly, especially in dim light' but VA looks fine.
Pelli–Robson chart: viewed at 1 m. Letters stay the same size but get fainter in groups of 3.
SPARCS: online grating test, works for people who can't read.
chunks.hook: VA = 'Can you read it?'  Contrast = 'Can you see it in fog?'

cards.q: Pelli–Robson is viewed at what distance?
Name 2 conditions where contrast drops but VA stays normal.
cards.a: Amblyopia, optic neuropathy (also some cataracts, higher-order aberrations).

chunks.title: Amsler grid
chunks.tldr: Amsler grid checks the central 20° of vision. Wavy lines → macula. Missing lines → nerve.
points: Used to screen and monitor macular disease. People at risk of CNV (wet AMD) should use one at home.
Hold at about 33 cm, wear reading glasses, pupils not dilated, do it before the slit lamp (bright light messes it up).
Cover one eye, stare at the central dot, and report any wavy, blurry or missing areas.
Wavy (metamorphopsia) → macular disease. Faint/missing but not wavy → optic neuropathy.
Missing corners or edges → think beyond the macula: glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa.
There are 7 charts. Chart 1 is standard: 5 mm squares, each = 1°. Chart 3 is red for toxic maculopathy and optic neuropathy. Chart 4 is dots only: tells a scotoma apart from distortion.
chunks.hook: Macula makes it Wavy; Nerve makes it Not there.
pearls: Red Amsler (chart 3) picks up colour desaturation in toxic maculopathy, optic neuropathy and chiasmal lesions.

cards.q: Patient sees wavy lines on Amsler. Where's the problem?
Which Amsler chart has only random dots, and why?
cards.a: Chart 4. No lines to bend, so it tells a scotoma apart from metamorphopsia.

chunks.title: Macula or optic nerve? Brightness & photostress
chunks.tldr: Two quick bedside tests: brightness drops in nerve disease, photostress recovery is slow in macular disease.
points: Light brightness comparison: shine a light in the good eye, then the bad eye. In optic neuropathy the light looks dimmer. Patient scores it 1–5.
Photostress test: bleach the macula with a light ~3 cm away for ~10 s, then time how long until they can read the old VA line again.
Normal recovery: 15–30 seconds.
Macular disease (mild CMO, CSR): slow, sometimes 50 s or more. Optic neuropathy: normal.
Plus lens test: CSR lifts the retina → causes a temporary hyperopic shift. A +1.00 lens shows it.
chunks.hook: Macula = slow to recharge (like a phone battery). Nerve = dim cable.

cards.q: Photostress recovery 60 s in the bad eye, 20 s in the good eye. Macula or nerve?
What refractive shift does CSR cause?
cards.a: Hypermetropic (hyperopic) shift, because the retina is lifted forward.

chunks.title: Colour vision
chunks.tldr: Optic nerve disease → red-green defects. Macular disease → blue-yellow defects. Ishihara only screens red-green.
points: Three cone types: blue (tritan), green (deuteran), red (protan).
Weak cone = '-anomaly' (protanomaly). Missing cone = '-anopia' (protanopia).
Most congenital colour-blind people are anomalous trichromats: all 3 cones present, one works badly.
Ishihara: screens congenital red-green only. If they can't read the test plate (and VA is OK) → think non-organic visual loss.
Hardy–Rand–Rittler: like Ishihara but catches all 3 defects (blue too).
Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue: actually 85 caps. Sensitive for congenital and acquired defects, but slow.
chunks.hook: Red-green = neRve. Blue-yellow = Back of the eye (macula).
pearls: How many caps in the '100-hue' test? 85.

cards.q: Patient can't read the Ishihara test plate, VA 6/6. Think?
Which colour test detects tritan (blue) defects: Ishihara or HRR?

chunks.title: Visual field basics: the hill of vision
chunks.tldr: The visual field is a hill: highest at the fovea, sloping down to the edges. A scotoma is a hole in it.
points: Field size: 50° up, 60° nasal, 70° down, 90° temporal.
Blind spot: 10–20° temporal, a little below the horizontal.
Isopter = a line joining points of equal sensitivity (like contour lines on a map).
Scotoma = area of lost vision with seeing area around it. Relative = dimmed. Absolute = gone.
Decibels (dB): higher dB = more sensitive (they saw a dimmer light). 10 dB = 1 log unit. Blind spot = 0 dB.
Sensitivity drops about 1 dB every 10 years after age 20.
Threshold = the brightness seen 50% of the time.
chunks.hook: Tem-po-ral is the bigger side: 90°. Remember '50-60-70-90' going up → nasal → down → temporal.

cards.q: Point A = 20 dB, point B = 30 dB. Which is more sensitive?
How far does the normal field go temporally?

chunks.title: Types of perimetry & test patterns
chunks.tldr: Static = light stays still and gets brighter. Kinetic = light moves in from outside. Glaucoma uses 24-2.
points: Static (Humphrey, Octopus): fixed spot, brightness changes. Standard in clinic (SAP).
Kinetic (Goldmann): fixed brightness, moved in from the edge until seen. Good for peripheral fields and patients who can't manage a machine.
Threshold testing: finds the exact dB at each point. Used to monitor glaucoma. Uses a 'staircase': big 4 dB steps, then fine 2 dB steps.
Suprathreshold: just 'can you see this normal-brightness spot?' Quick, used for screening.
SITA (Humphrey) and TOP (Octopus) = fast algorithms, nearly as accurate.
24-2 = routine glaucoma (24° temporal). 10-2 = central 10°, used for advanced glaucoma threatening fixation.
Esterman = binocular test for driving.
chunks.hook: Static = Still spot. Kinetic = Keeps moving.

cards.q: Advanced glaucoma with split fixation. Which pattern?
Which field test is used for driving licences?

chunks.title: Reading a Humphrey printout
chunks.tldr: Step 1: check reliability. Step 2: look at pattern deviation for focal loss. Step 3: check MD / PSD / GHT.
points: Fixation losses: light flashed in the blind spot and they pressed → not looking straight.
False positives: pressed when there was no light → 'trigger-happy'. Grey scale looks too pale/white.
False negatives: missed a bright light they saw before → tired or not paying attention. Grey scale looks like a clover leaf.
Cut-offs: SITA → FP/FN over ~15% is bad. Full-threshold → fixation loss over 20%, FP/FN over 33%.
Total deviation = compared with normal people your age. Pattern deviation = removes overall dimming (like cataract) to show focal defects.
MD = average overall loss. PSD = how patchy/focal the loss is → more specific for glaucoma.
VFI = whole field as %, normal 100%. GHT = compares top vs bottom half, for glaucoma only.
Each grey-scale shade = 5 dB.
chunks.hook: False Positive = Pale. False Negative = clover leaf (Not paying attention).
pearls: Cataract lowers total deviation everywhere but pattern deviation can still look normal.

cards.q: Grey scale looks abnormally white. Which reliability index is high?
MD or PSD: which is more specific for glaucoma?

chunks.title: Early-glaucoma fields & field errors
chunks.tldr: SAP only shows damage late. SWAP and FDT try to catch it earlier. Lots of simple things can fake a bad field.
points: SWAP: blue light on yellow background. Catches early glaucoma, but cataract ruins it (yellow lens blocks blue).
FDT (frequency doubling): flickering grating, tests big magnocellular cells lost early in glaucoma. Humphrey Matrix version.
Microperimetry (MAIA): tracks the fundus while testing the central 9°. Normal ≈ 18 dB. For macular disease.
Errors that fake defects: wrong date of birth, no near glasses, spectacle rim scotoma, small pupil (<3 mm → dilate), cataract, ptosis (top field lost), testing right after ophthalmoscopy.
chunks.hook: Before you call it glaucoma, check the 3 P's: Pupil, Ptosis, Patient details.

cards.q: Why isn't SWAP widely used?
cards.a: Cataract (yellow lens) reduces blue sensitivity, and the test is long.

cards.q: Pupil size below which you should dilate before perimetry?

chunks.title: Slit lamp lighting tricks
chunks.tldr: Four ways to light the cornea. Each one shows different things.
points: Direct illumination: narrow beam shows a cornea cross-section and lesion depth. Beam height measures size.
Red-free filter: makes red things look black → easier to see blood vessels. Cobalt blue → used with fluorescein.
Scleral scatter: shine on the limbus, light travels inside the cornea → shows subtle stromal haze and infiltrates.
Retroillumination: bounce light off iris or fundus → shows epithelial cysts, KPs, small vessels.
Specular reflection: shows the endothelium → cell density, guttata.
chunks.hook: Need to see endothelium/guttata? → Specular = 'Spec-tacular endothelium'.

cards.q: Which slit-lamp technique shows corneal guttata?
Best technique for subtle stromal haze?

chunks.title: Direct ophthalmoscope & slit-lamp fundus lenses
chunks.tldr: Direct ophthalmoscope = ×15 zoom, no 3D, tiny field. Slit-lamp lenses give an upside-down, flipped image.
points: Direct: right eye → your right hand, right eye. Approach from the temporal side, disc appears at ~3.5 cm.
Red reflex: use +15 D lens from 15–20 cm.
Hyperope → plus (green) lens. Myope → minus (red) lens.
Macula is about 2 disc diameters temporal to the disc.
60 D: high zoom, posterior pole. 90 D: wide field, small pupils (×1.3 disc correction). 78 D: all-rounder (×1.1).
Don't use contact lenses if there's a penetrating injury, hyphaema, or corneal infection.
chunks.hook: Bigger lens number = wider view, less zoom. 90 sees wide, 60 sees close.

cards.q: Magnification of the direct ophthalmoscope?
Which slit-lamp lens is best for small pupils: 60D or 90D?

chunks.title: Goldmann 3-mirror lens
chunks.tldr: Smaller mirror = further out in the retina. Put the mirror opposite the area you want to see.
points: Centre lens: posterior pole, 30°, upright view.
Biggest (oblong) mirror: 30° to the equator.
Middle (square) mirror: equator to ora serrata.
Smallest (dome) mirror: gonioscopy, far periphery, pars plana.
To see 12 o'clock, put the mirror at 6 o'clock.
Vertical view = upside down but not flipped left-right. Horizontal view = flipped left-right.
Needs coupling gel (methylcellulose), cup no more than half full.
chunks.hook: Mirrors get smaller as you go further out, like looking through a keyhole.

cards.q: Which 3-mirror part sees the ora serrata?
To view 9 o'clock retina, where's the mirror?

chunks.title: Indirect ophthalmoscopy (BIO) & fundus drawing
chunks.tldr: BIO sees through cloudier media and allows indentation. Magnification = 60 ÷ lens power.
points: 20 D: ×3, 45° field. The everyday lens.
28 D: ×2.27, 53°, good for small pupils. 40 D: ×1.5, 65°, for small children.
Patient lies down, pupils dilated, both eyes open. Look at the periphery first so they get used to the light.
Scleral indentation: see retina in front of the equator. Keep the indenter tangential. Pushing straight in hurts and can perforate thin sclera.
Drawing colours: detached retina = blue, flat retina = red, breaks = red outlined in blue, lattice = blue hatching, pigment = black, exudate = yellow, vitreous = green.
chunks.hook: 60 ÷ 20 = 3. Lower lens power → more zoom, smaller field.

cards.q: Magnification of a 20D BIO lens?
In fundus drawings, what colour is detached retina?

chunks.title: Goldmann applanation tonometry
chunks.tldr: Flatten a 3.06 mm circle of cornea. Dial reading × 10 = IOP in mmHg.
points: Imbert–Fick law: Pressure = Force ÷ Area.
At 3.06 mm, corneal stiffness and tear-film pull cancel out.
Anaesthetic + fluorescein, cobalt blue light at ~60°, start the dial at 1 (10 mmHg).
Two green half-circles (mires). Turn the dial until their inner edges just touch.
Mires should be about 10% of the arc thick.
Clean the prism: 2% hypochlorite kills adenovirus and HSV. Alcohol wipes don't.
chunks.hook: 3.06 mm: the 'magic circle' where all the forces balance.

cards.q: Dial reads 1.8. What's the IOP?
What diameter of cornea does Goldmann flatten?

chunks.title: Why the IOP reading might be wrong
chunks.tldr: Thick cornea → reads too high. Thin cornea → reads too low. Plus lots of technique errors.
points: Too much fluorescein → thick mires → reads high. Too little → reads low.
Squeezing the lids, your finger pressing the globe, thyroid eye muscles → falsely high.
Thin cornea (after LASIK, NTG) → falsely low. Thick cornea (ocular hypertension) → falsely high.
Corneal oedema → falsely low (soft, boggy cornea).
Astigmatism >3 D → average 2 readings at 90° apart, or line up the red mark with the minus axis.
Repeated readings → slight fall (massage effect). Tight collar / holding breath → higher.
Check calibration with the calibration bar before each clinic.
chunks.hook: Thick cornea = a thick wall, harder to push → overestimates.
pearls: Post-LASIK eyes are thin and altered → IOP is underestimated.

cards.q: After LASIK, is GAT IOP over- or under-estimated?
Too much fluorescein makes IOP read…?

chunks.title: Other tonometers & corneal hysteresis
chunks.tldr: Know which tonometer suits which patient. Low corneal hysteresis = higher glaucoma progression risk.
points: Air-puff (pneumotonometer): no touch, no drops → community screening. Average 3 readings.
Perkins: handheld Goldmann → bed-bound or anaesthetised patients.
Tono-Pen: works on scarred/oedematous corneas and through a soft contact lens.
iCare (rebound): small probe bounces off the cornea, no drops, can be used at home.
DCT (Pascal): less affected by corneal stiffness → closer to the true IOP.
Ocular Response Analyser: measures corneal hysteresis = how the cornea absorbs energy. Low hysteresis → more likely to progress. Also linked to how well prostaglandins lower IOP.
chunks.hook: Low hysteresis = 'poor shock absorber' = high risk.

cards.q: Best tonometer for an oedematous, irregular cornea?
Low corneal hysteresis means?

chunks.title: Central corneal thickness (CCT)
chunks.tldr: Normal CCT ≈ 540 ± 30 µm. Thin cornea hides a higher true IOP.
points: Measure with pachymetry or Orbscan.
Thin cornea → true IOP is higher than measured. Thick → true IOP is lower.
There's no reliable correction formula.
NTG patients tend to have thin corneas.
Always measure CCT in ocular hypertension: thin CCT = higher risk of turning into glaucoma.
Also a quick check of endothelial function (a swollen cornea gets thicker).
chunks.hook: Thin cornea = thin disguise: the real IOP is worse than it looks.

cards.q: OHT patient with CCT 490 µm: higher or lower risk of glaucoma?
Normal mean CCT?

chunks.title: Gonioscopy: why & how
chunks.tldr: You can't see the angle directly because of total internal reflection. A goniolens fixes that.
points: Light from the angle bounces back at the tear–air surface (critical angle ~46°). The goniolens removes that surface.
Indirect (mirror) lenses at the slit lamp: show the angle opposite the mirror.
Do it in a dark room, with a short beam that doesn't go through the pupil. Light shrinks the pupil and can make a closed angle look open.
Goldmann lens: needs coupling gel. Pressing hard on it → angle looks narrower.
Zeiss / Posner / Sussman (4-mirror): no gel needed → used for indentation.
Direct lenses (Koeppe, Swan–Jacob): patient lying down, often under GA → congenital glaucoma surgery.
AS-OCT and UBM help but don't replace gonioscopy.
chunks.hook: Gonioscopy in the dark: a bright light makes the angle look open when it isn't.

cards.q: Why can't you see the angle without a lens?
cards.a: Total internal reflection at the tear film–air interface.

cards.q: Which goniolens is used for indentation?

chunks.title: Indentation gonioscopy: apposition vs PAS
chunks.tldr: Push gently on the cornea. Angle opens → just touching (appositional). Stays shut → stuck (PAS).
points: Pressing pushes aqueous into the angle and pushes the iris back.
Appositional closure: iris just touching the angle → it opens.
Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS): iris stuck to the angle → stays closed.
Also helps tell a pigmented Schwalbe line apart from pigmented trabecular meshwork.
chunks.hook: Touching opens, stuck stays shut.

cards.q: On indentation the angle stays closed. Why?

chunks.title: Angle structures: front to back
chunks.tldr: From the front: Schwalbe line → trabecular meshwork → scleral spur → ciliary body.
points: Schwalbe line: where Descemet ends. White line. Find it with the corneal wedge (where the two light reflections meet). Pigment here = Sampaolesi line (e.g. PXF).
Trabecular meshwork (~600 µm): front part non-pigmented, back part pigmented = the working filter. Most pigmented inferiorly.
Schlemm canal: dark line behind the meshwork. Blood in it can be normal, or from low IOP / high episcleral venous pressure.
Scleral spur: white band, where the ciliary muscle attaches.
Ciliary body: grey-brown band. Wider in myopes, narrower in hyperopes.
Iris processes (normal, fine, about 1/3 of eyes) vs PAS (thick, reach further forward).
Any vessel crossing the scleral spur onto the meshwork = abnormal.
chunks.hook: "Some Teachers Study Carefully": Schwalbe, Trabeculum, Spur, Ciliary body.

cards.q: Most anterior angle structure?
A vessel crosses the scleral spur onto the TM. Normal?

chunks.title: Abnormal angle findings: the lists
chunks.tldr: Five things to spot in the angle: PAS, new vessels, too much pigment, trauma, blood in Schlemm.
points: PAS: primary angle closure, anterior uveitis, ICE syndrome.
New vessels: neovascular glaucoma, Fuchs heterochromic cyclitis, chronic anterior uveitis.
Heavy pigment: pigment dispersion, PXF, trauma, uveitis, after acute angle closure or YAG PI, melanoma/naevus, naevus of Ota.
Trauma: angle recession, trabecular dialysis, cyclodialysis, foreign body.
Blood in Schlemm canal: normal variant, carotid-cavernous fistula, Sturge–Weber, SVC obstruction (all raise episcleral venous pressure).
chunks.hook: Blood in Schlemm = back-pressure from the veins (CCF, Sturge–Weber, SVC).

cards.q: Name a uveitis with angle new vessels but usually no PAS.
3 causes of blood in Schlemm canal?
cards.a: Carotid-cavernous fistula, Sturge–Weber, SVC obstruction (or normal variant).
